0.title: The Gospel and the Slave: Paul's Letter to Philemon
0.overview:
Philemon is the most personal of Paul's surviving letters — a private request from a prisoner to a friend on behalf of a runaway slave. Twenty-five verses. No doctrinal argument, no community disputes, no eschatological vision. Just a man writing to a man about a third man, in the most careful and emotionally loaded prose Paul ever produced. That it was preserved in the canon at all — and that Marcion included it in his truncated collection — tells us that the early church recognized something here that went beyond private correspondence.

The situation is this: Onesimus, a slave belonging to the wealthy Colossian Christian Philemon, had run away. By Roman law, a runaway slave was a thief — he had stolen himself, depriving his master of the economic value of his labor, and possibly taken money or property in the process (v. 18 implies some kind of financial debt). He had somehow — the details are not given — come into contact with Paul, then imprisoned in Rome (or possibly Ephesus), and had been converted. He had become genuinely useful to Paul in his imprisonment. And Paul was sending him back, letter in hand.

The letter is a masterpiece of rhetorical strategy. Paul never commands Philemon to free Onesimus — he appeals, he hints, he presses, he places moral weight. He frames Onesimus as his own child (v. 10), his very heart (v. 12), a beloved brother (v. 16). He writes a personal financial guarantee for any debt (vv. 18–19). He expresses confidence that Philemon will do 'even more than I say' (v. 21). And he announces that he is coming to stay (v. 22). By the end of the letter, Philemon cannot refuse without refusing Paul himself — and refusing Paul means refusing the gospel they both serve.

The deepest theological claim of the letter is in v. 16: Onesimus is to be received 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother — both in the flesh and in the Lord.' The gospel does not erase social realities; it transforms them. Onesimus is still a man with a history, a legal status, a relationship with Philemon that has been damaged. But he is now a brother — in the flesh (as a human being) and in the Lord (as a fellow Christian). These two dimensions must operate simultaneously. Paul is not calling for the abolition of slavery in this letter; he is doing something more radical in the long run — he is planting a theological seed that makes slavery incompatible with Christian brotherhood.

1.title: Grace and a Brother: The Complete Letter
1.overview:
The letter unfolds in five movements: greeting (vv. 1–3), thanksgiving that both commends Philemon and establishes the relational capital Paul will spend (vv. 4–7), the appeal for Onesimus (vv. 8–16), the direct request and its financial guarantee (vv. 17–22), and final greetings (vv. 23–25). The movement from thanksgiving to appeal is calculated: Paul is building Philemon up before he asks anything of him, and the qualities he praises — love, faith, refreshing the hearts of the saints — are precisely the qualities the request will require.

The word splanchna (heart, deep affections — literally the inward parts, the seat of emotion in ancient physiology) appears three times and functions as the letter's emotional spine: in v. 7, the saints' hearts have been refreshed by Philemon; in v. 12, Paul sends Onesimus who is Paul's own heart; in v. 20, Paul asks Philemon to refresh Paul's heart. The chain is a deliberate literary strategy: establish Philemon as a heart-refresher, identify Onesimus as Paul's heart, ask Philemon to refresh Paul's heart by receiving Onesimus. The emotional argument is built into the structure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul writes as 'a prisoner for Christ Jesus', with Timothy, to Philemon their beloved fellow worker (v.1), to Apphia their sister and Archippus their fellow soldier, and to the church that meets in Philemon's house (v.2): grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ (v.3).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Credential He Sets Down

In almost every letter Paul opens with his office. Here he does not: he is 'a prisoner'. That is the first move in the most carefully constructed piece of persuasion in the New Testament. He is about to ask a slave-owner to do something extraordinary, and he begins by laying down the one credential that could have compelled it — he will mention the authority he is not using in verse 8, and the chains again in verse 9. Everything here is calculated, and all of it is calculated to leave Philemon free.

Note also a word that will work quietly throughout: 'the Lord Jesus Christ'. Kyrios is the ordinary Greek for master — the word a slave used of the man who owned him. Philemon is Onesimus's kyrios. Paul opens by naming a Kyrios above them both, and ends by asking Philemon to receive his slave as a brother, because they now share one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Four addressees, and the fourth is the strategy. 'The church in your house' means this is not a private note: Paul has addressed a letter about one man's slave to the entire congregation that meets in that man's living room — the people who will be sitting there when it is read aloud, and who will watch what Philemon does next. Apphia is very likely his wife, with a direct interest in a runaway's fate; Archippus is probably their son, the man told in Col 4:17 to fulfil his ministry.

Now: It should be said plainly that this is pressure, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing. But notice the kind. He does not command, threaten, or invoke his office. He makes the decision public, among brothers, and trusts what the gospel has already done in that house. The greeting is plural throughout — grace to you all. And 'God our Father' has already rearranged the relationships in the room before the argument begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house:
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus.' Not 'an apostle'. In almost every letter he opens with the office; here he sets it aside before he has written ten words.

That is the first move in the most carefully constructed piece of persuasion in the New Testament. Paul is about to ask a slave-owner to do something extraordinary, and he begins by laying down the one credential that could have compelled it. He will mention the authority he is not using in verse 8, and mention the chains again in verse 9. Everything in this letter is calculated, and all of it is calculated to leave Philemon free.

'And Timothy our brother' — a second name on a private letter about a domestic matter. Philemon is going to know that someone else has read this.

Then the addressees, and there are four. 'Philemon our beloved fellow worker' — a man Paul evidently knew well and had worked alongside, probably converted through him (v.19). 'Apphia our sister', very likely his wife, and as mistress of the house she had a direct interest in what happened to a runaway slave. 'Archippus our fellow soldier', probably their son, and the man told in Colossians 4:17 to fulfil the ministry he had received.

'And the church in your house.'

There is the whole strategy in five words. This is not a private note. Paul has addressed a letter about one man's slave to the entire congregation that meets in that man's living room — the people who will be sitting there when it is read aloud, and who will watch what Philemon does next.

It is worth being honest that this is pressure, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing. But notice the kind of pressure. He does not command, threaten, or invoke his office. He simply makes the decision public, among brothers, and trusts what the gospel has already done in this house.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.'

The standard greeting, and in this letter it is not a formality. Every word of what follows depends on it, and Paul will end on the same note in verse 25 — the letter is bracketed by grace, and grace is precisely what he is asking Philemon to extend.

'Grace' first, as always. The unearned favour that comes down before anything is deserved. Philemon has received it; Onesimus has received it; and the question the letter puts is whether a man who has been dealt with on those terms can bring himself to deal with someone else the same way.

'And peace' — shalom, not the absence of conflict merely but wholeness, things put right. Which is a pointed word to open a letter about a broken household. Something in that house is not whole. A man has run, a master has been wronged, and money is missing (v.18).

And there is a word in it that will do quiet work all the way through: 'the Lord Jesus Christ'. Kyrios is the ordinary Greek for master — it is the word a slave used of the man who owned him. Philemon is Onesimus's kyrios. Paul opens by naming a Kyrios above them both, and by the end he will ask Philemon to receive his slave as a brother, because they now share one.

Note also that the greeting is plural throughout — grace to you all. Paul is still speaking to the room.

'From God our Father' is quietly doing work too. If God is Father to Philemon and to the congregation, and Onesimus is now Paul's child in the faith (v.10), then the relationships in that house have already been rearranged before the argument begins. Paul does not announce it. He lets the ordinary language of the greeting carry it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God always when he remembers Philemon in prayer (v.4), because he hears of his love and of the faith he has toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints (v.5). He prays that the sharing of Philemon's faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for Christ's sake (v.6) — for Paul has derived much joy and comfort from his love, since the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through him (v.7).
verseByVerse.theology:
An Argument Built Out of a Man's Own Character

Paul does not begin by telling Philemon what he ought to be. He tells him truthfully what he already is, and then asks him to be it consistently — which is far harder to refuse than a rebuke, and treats him as an adult and a Christian rather than a problem to be managed.

Watch the two key words of verse 7, because the letter is assembled from them. 'Hearts' is splanchna, the gut-word for where feeling is actually located; 'refreshed' means to give rest to, as you would to an exhausted animal or a tired traveller. In verse 12 Paul will call Onesimus his own splanchna — my very heart — and in verse 20 he will ask Philemon to refresh his heart in Christ. The two terms that describe this man's established reputation are, thirteen verses later, applied to a runaway slave.

Verse 6 is the hardest sentence to translate, and read in context the prayer is not general: that the fellowship Philemon's faith creates would work, issuing in a full recognition of what is his in Christ. Paul is praying, in advance, for the very thing he is about to ask.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Consider how this news reached a prison in Rome. 'I hear of your love' — somebody told him, and the likeliest somebody is standing beside him as he writes. Onesimus had every reason to describe his master unfavourably, and what came through was a report of a man known for loving all the saints.

Now: 'For all the saints' is the word the whole letter turns on. Philemon has a reputation for loving every believer he meets — and Paul is about to present him with a saint he had not counted, a man who is now among the 'all' and who used to serve his dinner. The method is worth learning by anyone who has to ask something hard of another Christian: name the grace already at work in them, accurately and without flattery, and then ask them to extend it to the case they had excluded.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers.' Paul's thanksgivings are never merely polite, and this one is doing two things at once: it is sincere, and it is establishing the ground on which the request will be made.

What he thanks God for is stated in verse 5, and the order in the Greek is worth noticing: 'your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints.'

The four terms are arranged in a cross-pattern — love and faith, then Jesus and the saints — so that faith belongs primarily to Christ and love primarily to the saints. Paul has heard, in a Roman prison, that this man in a small Phrygian town is known for both.

And 'for all the saints' is the word the whole letter turns on. All of them. Philemon has a reputation for loving every believer he meets.

And consider how the news reached a prison in Rome. 'I hear of your love' — somebody told him, and the most likely somebody is standing beside him as he writes. Onesimus had every reason to describe his master unfavourably, and the report Paul received was of a man known for loving all the saints. Whatever else the runaway said about that household, this is what came through.

Paul is not flattering him. He is describing him accurately and then, in a few verses, presenting him with a saint he had not counted — a man who is now among the 'all', and who used to serve his dinner.

This is the method of the whole letter and it is worth learning. Paul does not begin by telling Philemon what he ought to be. He begins by telling him truthfully what he already is, and then asks him to be it consistently. That is a far harder thing to refuse than a rebuke, and it treats the man as an adult and a Christian rather than a problem to be managed.

verseByVerse.quote: and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ. For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ.'

It is the most compressed sentence in the letter and the hardest to translate. 'Sharing' is koinonia — partnership, having in common — and the phrase most likely means the fellowship that your faith creates, the shared life it produces with other believers.

'May become effective' is the working word, from which we get 'energy': that the partnership would actually do something. And the aim is 'the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ' — a deeper recognition of what we already possess in him.

Read it in context and the prayer is not general. Paul is praying that Philemon's fellowship with other Christians would work itself out into a full recognition of what is his in Christ — and the very next paragraph will present him with a specific case in which that recognition has to be exercised. He is praying, in advance, for the thing he is about to ask.

Then verse 7, which is the warmest thing in the letter and also the most strategic: 'the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.'

'Hearts' is splanchna — the gut-word Paul used of his own longing at Philippians 1:8, the inward parts where feeling is actually located. And 'refreshed' means to give rest to, to relieve; it is what you do for an exhausted animal or a tired traveller.

Now watch what Paul does with these two words. In verse 12 he will call Onesimus his own splanchna — my very heart. And in verse 20 he will ask Philemon to refresh his heart in Christ. He has taken the two words that describe Philemon's established reputation and, thirteen verses later, asked him to apply both to a runaway slave. The letter's argument is being assembled out of the man's own character.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Though bold enough in Christ to command what is required (v.8), Paul prefers for love's sake to appeal — as an old man and now a prisoner (v.9) — for his child Onesimus, whose father he became in prison (v.10). Formerly useless, he is now useful to them both (v.11). Paul is sending him back, sending his very heart (v.12); he would gladly have kept him to serve in Philemon's place (v.13), but preferred to do nothing without consent, so that his goodness might not be by compulsion but of his own accord (v.14). Perhaps he was parted from him for a while so that he might have him back for ever (v.15) — no longer as a bondservant but more than one, as a beloved brother, especially to Paul but how much more to Philemon, both in the flesh and in the Lord (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Goodness by Compulsion Is Not Goodness

Verse 14 governs the whole letter and states a principle far larger than the case. Paul could have kept Onesimus; he could have written a letter Philemon could not refuse. He did neither, because goodness extracted under pressure has the shape of the thing and none of the substance. That is a considerable statement about how God deals with people: he could compel obedience and does not, for the same reason — what he is after is not conduct but a willing heart, and compulsion cannot produce one.

Verse 16 is the sentence the letter exists to deliver, and it repays exactness. Paul does not command manumission. He says something a slave society could not survive being told: whatever the legal status, the category has been superseded — 'no longer as a bondservant', that is not how you may now regard him. And 'both in the flesh and in the Lord' refuses to confine the brotherhood to the assembly; it must hold in the household, in the daily arrangements. Where that was believed, the institution eventually became unthinkable.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The runaway got as far as Rome — the obvious place to disappear in a population of a million — and there met the one man in the empire most likely to send him home. Verse 11 is a pun: the name Onesimus means useful, a common slave name. Your Useful was useless; now he is what his name always claimed. Note that Paul concedes the whole charge rather than rewriting the history — he was useless, and he stole — and asks for him anyway, on entirely different grounds. And the 'perhaps' of verse 15 is exquisite: Paul offers Philemon a way of reading his own loss, and offers it tentatively, with a passive verb ('he was parted from you') that leaves room for another hand without pretending nothing was done (cf. Gen 45:5-8).

Now: Verse 8 is a masterpiece of restraint, and note that Paul does not conceal the authority he is withholding — he names it, so Philemon knows exactly what is being set down. That is the opposite of manipulation: a man who quietly forgoes a right leaves the other person guessing. What he puts on the table instead is personal — an old man, in chains, asking. There is a real difference between the pressure of authority and the pressure of affection, and only one of them leaves a man free.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you—I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus—
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you.'

Here is the hinge of the letter, and it is a masterpiece of restraint. Paul states plainly that he has the authority to give an order — 'what is required' implies the outcome is not in doubt — and then declines to use it.

Note that he does not conceal the authority. He names it, so that Philemon knows exactly what is being withheld. That is not manipulation; it is the opposite of it. A man who quietly forgoes a right leaves the other person guessing. Paul puts it on the table and then sets it down where it can be seen.

'For love's sake I prefer to appeal.' The verb is parakaleo — to call alongside, to beg. Command produces compliance; appeal produces something else, and Paul wants the something else. He will say why in verse 14: goodness by compulsion is not goodness.

Then the two things he does put on the table, and they are unashamedly personal: 'I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus.'

He is trading on his age and his chains. Some have found this uncomfortable, as if it were emotional leverage. But there is a real difference between the pressure of authority and the pressure of affection, and only one of them leaves a man free. Paul is not saying 'you must'. He is saying 'this is an old man in prison, asking you'.

And there is something worth seeing in an apostle willing to appear as an old man rather than an office. He has spent his life insisting on his apostleship when the gospel was at stake. Here, where only a slave's future is at stake, he lays it down without a murmur.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment. (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus.'

Note the order of the Greek: the appeal, the relationship, and only then the name. Philemon has to hear 'my child' before he hears which child. By the time the name lands — the name of the man who robbed him and ran — Paul has already claimed him as a son.

'Whose father I became in my imprisonment.' The runaway got as far as Rome, the obvious place to disappear in a population of a million, and there met the one man in the empire most likely to send him home. Whatever Onesimus thought he was doing, he ran directly into the gospel.

Then verse 11, and it is a pun: 'Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.'

The name Onesimus means useful — a common slave name, given for the obvious reason. So Paul is saying: your Useful was useless; now he is what his name always claimed. The wordplay is gentle and it is also an admission. Paul does not pretend the man was a good servant badly treated. He was useless, and he stole, and Paul says so.

That candour is essential to the letter's integrity. Paul is not asking Philemon to pretend nothing happened or to accept a rewritten history. He concedes the whole charge — and then asks for the man anyway, on entirely different grounds.

'Useful to you and to me.' Not merely reformed in the abstract. Paul has found him genuinely useful in prison, and expects Philemon to find the same. Grace does not only forgive a man's past; it makes him worth something, and Paul is prepared to put his own experience of the man behind the claim.

verseByVerse.quote: I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart. I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel, but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I am sending him back to you.' Three words that decide everything, and they come before any of the pleading.

Paul does not hide Onesimus, or argue that his conversion has cancelled the legal position, or ask Philemon to waive his claim from a safe distance. He puts the man on the road to Colossae with a letter in his hand. Under Roman law a returning fugitive could be branded, flogged, or worse, and both men knew it. The whole appeal is made after the risk has already been taken.

'Sending my very heart' — splanchna again, the word from verse 7. Philemon refreshes the hearts of the saints; Paul is sending him his own. To receive Onesimus badly is now to injure Paul in a place he has named.

'I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment.' Paul wanted him and says so plainly. There is no pretence that returning him was easy or that Onesimus was dispensable.

'On your behalf' is delicate. Paul is suggesting that had Onesimus stayed, his service would have counted as Philemon's — which quietly proposes a way for a slave-owner to be generous rather than merely deprived.

Then verse 14, and it is the sentence that governs the whole letter: 'but I preferred to do nothing without your consent, in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.'

Paul could have kept him. He could have written a letter Philemon could not refuse. He did neither, and the reason is stated as a principle: goodness extracted under pressure is not goodness. It has the shape of the thing and none of the substance.

That is why this letter argues instead of commanding, and it is a considerable statement about how God deals with people. He could compel obedience and does not, for the same reason — what he is after is not conduct but a willing heart, and compulsion cannot produce one.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever.'

The 'perhaps' is exquisite. Paul is offering Philemon a way of reading his own loss, and he offers it tentatively. He does not claim to know the mind of God about a theft in Colossae. He suggests it.

And notice the passive: 'he was parted from you.' Not 'he ran away', which is what happened. The passive leaves room for another hand behind the running — the same delicacy as Joseph telling his brothers that God sent him to Egypt (Gen 45:5-8) without pretending they had not sold him.

'For a while' against 'forever'; and the Greek for 'for a while' is literally 'for an hour'. A few months of loss set against an eternity of brotherhood. Paul is asking Philemon to do the arithmetic.

Then verse 16, which is the sentence the whole letter exists to deliver: 'no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother.'

Read it carefully, because Paul does not quite say what we might wish he said. He does not command manumission. He says something that is in the long run more corrosive: whatever Onesimus's legal status, the category has been superseded. 'No longer as a bondservant' — that is not how you may now regard him — 'but more than' one.

'Especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.' In the flesh — in the actual household, in the daily arrangements, not merely in some spiritual realm where equality costs nothing. Paul will not let the brotherhood be confined to Sunday.

It is worth being clear about what this does and does not do. It is not an abolition decree, and the New Testament nowhere issues one. It is something a slave society could not survive being told: that the man in the kitchen is your brother, in the house as well as in the assembly. Where that was believed, the institution eventually became unthinkable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — Receive Him as You Would Receive Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If Philemon considers Paul his partner, he is to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul (v.17). If the man has wronged him or owes him anything, it is to be charged to Paul's account (v.18) — written in his own hand, a promise to repay, to say nothing of Philemon owing him his own self (v.19). Yes, brother: let Paul have some benefit from him in the Lord, and refresh his heart in Christ (v.20). He writes confident of his obedience, knowing he will do even more than is asked (v.21) — and asks him to prepare a guest room, hoping to be given to them through their prayers (v.22).

Epaphras his fellow prisoner sends greetings (v.23), as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, his fellow workers (v.24). The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit (v.25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Charge That to My Account

Verses 17-19 enact a doctrine rather than expounding one. A man owes a debt he cannot pay; a third party assumes it in writing, at his own cost; and the offended party is asked to receive the debtor as though he were the one who paid — 'receive him as you would receive me'. Paul has spent his letters arguing justification. Here he simply does it, in a domestic matter, for one man, and never points at the parallel.

'Charge that to my account' is commercial language, and verse 19 is a legally recognisable form of words — a signed promissory note, written into a letter the whole church will hear read. The IOU is public and binding. Then the lightest touch in the letter: 'to say nothing of your owing me even your own self', mentioned while he insists he is not mentioning it. What is a household purse against a man's soul?
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Reckon what verse 17 would cost. Philemon has other slaves, and they will be watching; he has neighbours who own slaves, and they will hear. A master who welcomes a thieving runaway to his own table has, in the eyes of every household in Colossae, lost control of his — and that society had no mechanism for admiring him for it. Paul is not asking for a private act of forgiveness but for a public humiliation. Note too that 'benefit' in verse 20 is onaimen, from the same root as the name: a second pun, and the argument is still being made in the man's own name.

Now: Every reader wonders what the 'more' of verse 21 is, and the obvious candidate is freedom. Paul has carefully not asked for manumission — he asked for a brother to be received as a brother — and here leaves a door open without walking through it, because naming it would make it a command and destroy what verse 14 insisted on. Then verse 22 is the gentlest possible accountability: prepare a guest room, because I am coming to see how this turned out. A decision you must explain to someone's face is a different decision from one made at a distance. We are never told what Philemon did — but a document recording a refused request would not have been copied and treasured by the church that heard it read.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.'

This is the request. Everything before it has been preparation and everything after is detail, and it is one sentence long.

'Partner' is koinonos — the koinonia root from verse 6, where Paul prayed that the sharing of Philemon's faith would become effective. Here is where it becomes effective. A partner in the ancient world was someone with whom you held things in common, often in business; and Paul is invoking a relationship Philemon would certainly acknowledge in order to draw a conclusion he might not.

'Receive him as you would receive me.' Not forgive him. Not take him back. Receive him as Paul — with the welcome, the seat, the standing that an apostle and old friend would be given if he walked through the door.

Sit for a moment with what that asks. A slave who has robbed his owner and run is to be welcomed home as though he were the most honoured guest the house could receive. There is no half-measure available; Paul has named the standard and it is himself.

It is worth reckoning what it would cost. Philemon has other slaves, and they will be watching. He has neighbours who own slaves, and they will hear. A master who welcomes a thieving runaway to his own table has, in the eyes of every household in Colossae, lost control of his — and there was no mechanism in that society for such a man to be admired for it. Paul is not asking for a private act of forgiveness. He is asking Philemon to accept a public humiliation.

Which is presumably why the request is framed as it is. 'If you consider me your partner' is a condition Paul expects to be granted — the Greek assumes it is true. He is not asking whether Philemon will obey an apostle. He is asking what a partnership is worth when it becomes expensive.

And there is a deeper pattern in it, which the New Testament makes explicit elsewhere. One stands in the place of another, and the offender is received on the standing of the one who intercedes. Philemon is being asked to accept Onesimus on Paul's account — which is precisely how Philemon himself was accepted, and the next two verses will make the parallel unmistakable.

verseByVerse.quote: If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.'

The 'if' is a courtesy; the debt was real, and everyone reading knew it. Runaway slaves did not generally travel to Rome without funds. Paul concedes the wrong without dwelling on it and then does the only thing that actually resolves it.

'Charge that to my account' is commercial language — put it on my ledger. Paul is not asking Philemon to absorb the loss or to be big about it. He is offering to pay.

Then verse 19, and Paul takes the pen from his secretary: 'I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it.' That is a legally recognisable form of words — a signed promissory note, written into a letter that the whole church will hear read. The IOU is public and binding.

The theology in this is impossible to miss and Paul does not point at it. A man who owes a debt he cannot pay; a third party who assumes it in writing at his own cost; and the offended party asked to receive the debtor as though he were the one who paid. Paul has spent his letters arguing that doctrine, and here he simply does it, in a domestic matter, for a single man.

Then the lightest touch in the letter: 'to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.'

He has just offered to pay Philemon's debt — and mentions, while insisting he is not mentioning it, that Philemon owes him everything, because Paul brought him the gospel. It is done with a smile, and it is unanswerable. What is the theft of a household purse against a man's own soul?

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Yes, brother' — and the word matters, because it is the very term he has just asked Philemon to apply to Onesimus (v.16). Paul, Philemon and Onesimus are now all in the same category, and the letter has quietly put them there.

'I want some benefit from you in the Lord.' The verb is onaimen, and it is from the same root as the name Onesimus. Paul is punning again, for the second time: let me have some Onesimus from you. Even here, at the close, the argument is being made in the man's name.

'Refresh my heart in Christ.' Both words come back from verse 7 — refresh, and splanchna. Philemon has refreshed the hearts of the saints; Paul has sent him his own heart in the person of Onesimus; now he asks for the thing this man is already famous for, in the one case where it will cost him.

Then verse 21: 'Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.'

Every commentator has wondered what the 'more' is, and the obvious candidate is freedom. Paul has carefully not asked for manumission — he asked for a brother to be received as a brother — and here he leaves a door open without walking through it. He will not name it, because naming it would make it a command and destroy the very thing verse 14 insisted on.

And then verse 22, which is the gentlest possible pressure: 'prepare a guest room for me.'

Paul is coming. Whatever Philemon decides, the apostle expects to walk into that house and see how it turned out. It is said warmly and as a hope resting on their prayers — and it is also, unmistakably, an accountability. A decision you will have to explain to someone's face is a different decision from one you make at a distance.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you, and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five names, and they are the same circle that appears at the close of Colossians — which is one of the reasons the two letters are thought to have travelled together, carried by Tychicus with Onesimus walking beside him (Col 4:7-9).

'Epaphras, my fellow prisoner' — the man who founded the Colossian church (Col 1:7) and wrestled in prayer for them (Col 4:12). 'Mark' — the deserter of Acts 15, restored. 'Aristarchus' — Paul's fellow prisoner from Thessalonica. 'Demas' — who is still faithful here, and who will one day leave, in love with this present world (2 Tim 4:10). And 'Luke', who would be the last one with him.

These are witnesses, and Philemon knew every one of them. The list is affectionate and it is also, like everything else in this letter, quietly public.

'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.' And 'your' is plural: the whole household, the whole church in that room. Grace opened the letter (v.3) and closes it, which is exactly right, because grace is what the letter has been asking for from beginning to end — that a man who has been received without deserving it should receive somebody else the same way.

We are never told what Philemon did. The letter's survival is itself the strongest evidence: a document recording a request that had been refused would not have been copied and treasured by the church that heard it read.

There is a further hint, though it can be put no higher. Some fifty years later Ignatius of Antioch wrote to the church at Ephesus in warm praise of their bishop — a man named Onesimus, and he plays on the same word, calling him one who is 'beyond measure useful'. Whether it is the same man cannot be proved, and the name was common enough. But it is a pleasant thought that the runaway ended his life as a bishop, and that the letter asking for his freedom was kept safe by the churches he served.
